look_here_first: Start with the TWIG, not the leaf: regular corky wings on branches are the fastest clue. Then check whether those wings stop abruptly at a leaf node, look for pointed double-serrate leaves, and use SPRING flowers/samaras to separate winged elm from fall-fruiting cedar elm.

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: paired corky wings commonly develop on young and older branches

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: wings usually terminate abruptly at leaf nodes rather than flowing continuously around them

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: leaves relatively small, pointed, and double-serrate with pinnate elm venation

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: flowers before or around leaf-out in spring

key_traits.label: Identification
key_traits.text: small spring samaras with hairy/ciliate margins

key_traits.label: Elm training
key_traits.text: Winged elm vs cedar elm: twig wings overlap, so use the node plus season. Winged elm usually has regular wings that end at the node and reproduces in spring; cedar elm may carry corky ridges around nodes and reproduces in late summer-fall.
